name: Blow-dry and volumizing routine
lead: A blow-dry and volumizing routine is a hair-styling practice in which hair is dried with a handheld dryer, often while being lifted or directed upward at the roots, to give the hairstyle more height and body. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and grooming circles as a low-cost way to change the apparent fullness of the hair.

Hair dryers work by passing air from a fan over an electric heating element. Styling with them is described as forming temporary hydrogen bonds in each hair strand, which weaken with humidity and are undone by washing.[1] Dryers commonly include a concentrator nozzle, a diffuser and a cool-air setting that is described as helping to set a style.[1]

No published clinical studies were found that test blow-drying routines for volume. General hair-care references note that heat from dryers and hot irons can leave hair dry and brittle when overused.[2]

paras: In a volumizing blow-dry, hair is typically dried while sections are lifted away from the scalp or directed upward, so that the hair sets in a raised position. A cool-air burst at the end is described in dryer references as helping to hold the shape and reduce frizz.[1]

Attachments change how the airflow reaches the hair. A concentrator narrows the airflow to focus heat and speed up drying, while a comb nozzle combines a concentrator with comb-like teeth.[1] A diffuser spreads the airflow and is described as drying hair more slowly, at a lower temperature and with less disturbance.[1]

An early seated hair dryer was developed by French stylist Alexandre Godefroy in 1888, and handheld dryers appeared around 1920. Safety guidelines for dryers were issued in the 1970s in the United States.[1]

General hair-care references state that hair overheated by dryers and hot irons can become dry and brittle and that heat is among the traumas that can lead to split ends.[2] A 1982 dermatology report described contact allergy to nickel from a blow-dry hair brush, an example of tool-related skin reactions.[3]

quick.overview:
A blow-dry and volumizing routine means drying hair with a dryer while lifting it at the roots so the style sets with more height. It is a styling technique rather than a treatment.

No published studies were found that test it for volume. The effect is temporary.
quick.mechanism: Dryers are described as setting hair by forming temporary hydrogen bonds in each strand, which humidity and washing reverse. Nozzles and diffusers change how air and heat reach the hair.
quick.risks: Hair-care references note that heat from dryers can leave hair dry and brittle with heavy use. Tool-related skin reactions, such as nickel contact allergy from a brush, have been reported in case literature.
